onggi.name: Onggi
onggi.summary: Korean earthenware used for centuries as tableware and storage, dating back to around 4000–5000 BCE, including unglazed and dark-glazed types.

j-mon-period.name: Jōmon period
j-mon-period.summary: Era in Japanese history from about 14,000 to 300 BC when Japan was inhabited by the Jōmon culture, known for bone, stone and shell tools and jewelry, pottery and lacquerware.

jeulmun-pottery-period.name: Jeulmun pottery period
jeulmun-pottery-period.summary: An archaeological era in Korean prehistory lasting from about 8000 to 1500 BCE, named for its distinctive comb-patterned pottery, covering Korea's Mesolithic and Neolithic stages.

edward-s-morse.name: Edward S. Morse
edward-s-morse.summary: American zoologist and archaeologist (1838–1925) known as the "Father of Japanese archaeology."

j-mon-people.name: Jōmon people
j-mon-people.summary: Prehistoric hunter-gatherer culture in the Japanese archipelago from about 14,000 to 300 BC, known for foraging, fishing and hunting, later largely assimilated by Yayoi migrants.

amsa-dong-prehistoric-site.name: Amsa-dong Prehistoric Site
amsa-dong-prehistoric-site.summary: An archaeological site and open-air museum in Seoul showing evidence of human habitation from 3,000 to 4,000 years ago, including comb-pattern pottery and early farming settlements.

j-mon-pottery.name: Jōmon pottery
j-mon-pottery.summary: Ancient earthenware made in Japan's Jōmon period, among the earliest pottery known, decorated with rope-pressed cord patterns; later forms include elaborate flame and crown-shaped vessels.

dog.name: Dogū
dog.summary: Small humanoid and animal clay figurines made in Japan's later Jōmon period (14,000–400 BCE); their purpose remains unknown.

baiyue.name: Baiyue
baiyue.summary: Various ethnic groups living across southern China and northern Vietnam during the 1st millennia BC and AD, known for short hair, tattoos and skilled seafaring, later assimilated into Chinese culture.

altai-mountains.name: Altai Mountains
altai-mountains.summary: Mountain range in Central Asia where Russia, China, Mongolia, and Kazakhstan meet, home to a sparse, ethnically diverse population including Turkic peoples and Mongols.

haplogroup-c-m8.name: Haplogroup C1a1
haplogroup-c-m8.summary: A rare Y-chromosome lineage found in about 6% of modern Japanese men, once thought to descend from the Jōmon people, though recent Jōmon-era DNA findings have challenged that link.

haplogroup-c-m217.name: Haplogroup C2
haplogroup-c-m217.summary: A major Y-chromosome lineage found mostly in Central Asia and eastern Siberia, at high frequency among Mongolians, Kazakhs and other Central Asian and Siberian peoples, and possibly linked to Genghis Khan's direct male descendants.

ka-island.name: Ka Island
ka-island.summary: North Korean island in the Pansong Archipelago in West Korea Bay, forming part of Cholsan County.

primorsky-krai.name: Primorsky Krai
primorsky-krai.summary: A Russian federal subject in the Far East bordering North Korea, ceded to Russia by Qing China in 1860; its administrative center is Vladivostok.

manchuria.name: Manchuria
manchuria.summary: A historical region of Northeast Asia covering present-day Northeast China and parts of the Russian Far East, the homeland of the Manchu people who founded the Qing dynasty.

dai-yamamoto-i-site.name: Ōdai Yamamoto I Site
dai-yamamoto-i-site.summary: A Jōmon archaeological site in Aomori Prefecture, northern Japan, where 1998 excavations uncovered earthenware fragments dated to about 14,500 BCE, among the earliest known pottery, marking the start of the Incipient Jōmon period.
